newsitem.title: IRAN: No woman president in Iran yet, but minister maybe.
newsitem.headline: No woman president in Iran yet, but minister maybe.

text.p: President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani's daughter, the most prominent woman in Iranian politics, said on Thursday she hoped the next president would appoint a female minister.
Faezeh Hashemi, elected to parliament in March 1996 by the second largest majority in the Islamic republic's national elections, said it was too early for Iran to have a female president.
But she added: "I do hope and believe that we can have a woman minister and it would depend on the elected president, whoever that would be."

Hashemi was speaking at a news conference in Tehran at the end of campaigning for Friday's election to replace Rafsanjani, who must by law retire from the presidency in August after eight years in office.
She has campaigned actively for Mohammad Khatami, a candidate backed by pro-Rafsanjani centrists, who is the main rival of conservative Parliament Speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri.

Election campaigning is banned during the 24 hours before voting but Hashemi said young people believed Khatami had a better understanding of their demands because of his background as a former culture and Islamic guidance minister.

Asked whether there could be a backlash among conservative clergymen to more rights for women, she said: "I don't believe so since there is no opposition from Islam towards the activities of women ... generally I can say that there is no opposition or impediment towards the activities of women in religion."

Asked about the Islamic republic's rules requiring women to wear hejab or covering from head to toe, Hashemi said "administering the Islamic rules and regulations in our society have created confidence and trust towards our women which has enabled them to be active in all different social fields from the most remote areas of our country and the rural areas.
"Therefore, I as an Iranian woman would like to say we do feel quite comfortable with this hejab or Islamic cover and we do consider it an element of growth for our people and our society.
"The hejab has not only not created any limitations but by giving trust and confidence and security has enabled us to have a more prominent and active role in our societies."

Hashemi also spoke in favour of polygamy, saying "Because of the natural calamities and disasters and wars there are occasions when the number of men are much less than the women, and this would help the women with no support."
But it should be in accordance with the spirit of the Moslem holy book the Koran, which permits a man to have up to four wives, she said.
